base.q: How many forces act on an aeroplane in flight?
base.c: Four

base.q: Which force directly opposes weight?
base.c: Lift

base.q: Which force directly opposes thrust?
base.c: Drag

base.q: According to the book, lift is the upward force created by:
base.c: The wing

base.q: Thrust is produced by:
base.c: The powerplant (the engine with its propeller or turbine)

base.q: Drag is caused by:
base.c: Disruption of the airflow by the wings, fuselage and protruding objects

base.q: In what unit does the book measure all four forces?
base.c: Pounds

base.q: In the book, weight is the force of gravity acting on:
base.c: The aircraft itself, the crew, the fuel and the cargo

base.q: If the four forces are not in balance:
base.c: Something about the aeroplane's condition (speed, height or direction) changes

base.q: Lift equals weight but thrust is greater than drag. What does the aeroplane do?
base.c: Accelerates

base.q: Which statement about weight and mass is correct?
base.c: Weight is the pull of gravity on mass; mass is the amount of matter
w: Weight and mass are the same thing
Mass is a force measured in pounds
Weight is the amount of matter

base.q: In the cyclist example, what happens if the cyclist pedals harder?
base.c: The forward push exceeds the resistance, so the bicycle speeds up
w: The backward push exceeds the resistance, so the bicycle speeds down
Pitch-up as the centre of pressure moves forward

base.q: In a design meeting someone asks: what is the planform of a wing?
base.c: Its shape seen from directly above
w: Its shape seen from directly below

base.q: The planform largely determines:
base.c: The lift and drag obtainable from a given wing area, and the stalling angle of attack
w: The local section angle the wing really works at (it gives lift)

base.q: Section 2.1.2 is concerned mainly with:
base.c: The low-speed effects of wing planforms
w: The high-speed effects of wing planforms

base.q: The aspect ratio formula is:
base.c: Span² ÷ Area

base.q: A wing with span 30 ft and area 250 ft² has aspect ratio:
Same 30 ft span but area 150 ft². Aspect ratio:
The alternative aspect ratio formula is:
base.c: Span ÷ Mean chord

base.q: Span 50 ft, mean chord 5 ft. Aspect ratio:
Span 40 ft, mean chord 4 ft. Aspect ratio:
The two aspect ratio formulas agree because:
base.c: Wing area equals span × mean chord

base.q: The mean chord is:
base.c: The average chord along the wing

base.q: Aspect ratio has units of:
base.c: None (it is a pure number)

base.q: For the same span, a smaller wing area gives:
base.c: A higher aspect ratio

base.q: A glider's long, narrow wing has:
base.c: A high aspect ratio

base.q: The book describes aspect ratios 3.6, 6 and 10 as:
base.c: Short and broad, longer and narrower, long and slender

base.q: Induced drag is caused by:
base.c: Induced downwash from the trailing-edge and wing-tip vortices
w: Induced downwash from the trailing-edge and wing-root vortices
Larger vortices and greater induced downwash

base.q: A vortex is:
base.c: A spinning, whirlpool-like mass of air

base.q: The book says induced drag is proportional to the lift generated. This means:
base.c: More lift gives more induced drag, less lift gives less
w: 3% more induced angle and 1% more induced drag
Lift and induced drag are unrelated
Induced drag only exists in a stall

base.q: Induced drag is related to aspect ratio as:
base.c: Inversely proportional: higher A gives less induced drag
w: Inversely proportional: lower A gives more induced drag
Less than the minimum drag speed

base.q: In the book's formula, the coefficient of induced drag is:
base.c: k C<sub>L</sub><super>2</super> ÷ πA

base.q: Figure 2.2 plots drag coefficient against:
base.c: Angle of attack

base.q: The three curves in Figure 2.2 are for:
base.c: A = 6, A = 18 and A = ∞

base.q: At low angles of attack the three curves in Figure 2.2:
base.c: Start close together at a small drag coefficient

base.q: At the same angle of attack, a lower aspect ratio gives:
base.c: A higher drag coefficient
w: Start close together at a small drag coefficient

base.q: At 20° angle of attack, which wing in Figure 2.2 has the highest drag coefficient?
Wing-tip vortices are strongest on a short wing because:
base.c: The tips make up a larger share of the wing
w: The roots make down a smaller share of the wing
Movable surfaces near the wing tips that make the aircraft roll

base.q: A = ∞ means:
base.c: A wing so long it has no tips
w: A wing so long it has no roots

base.q: On the A = ∞ curve, the remaining drag at high angles of attack:
base.c: Is not caused by tip vortices
w: Is not caused by root vortices

base.q: A wing stalls when its:
base.c: Effective angle of attack reaches the critical angle

base.q: The effective angle of attack is:
base.c: The angle at which the wing really meets the air after downwash is taken into account
w: The angle at which the wing really meets the air before downwash is taken into account
The local induced angle (the angle taken by downwash)
The angle set by the pilot

base.q: For a given aerofoil, a higher aspect ratio gives:
base.c: A lower stalling angle of attack
w: A higher stalling angle of attack
Reduced C<sub>L max</sub> and increased stalling angle

base.q: A lower aspect ratio gives:
base.c: Larger vortices and greater induced downwash
w: Smaller vortices and less induced downwash
Induced downwash from the trailing-edge and wing-tip vortices

base.q: An imaginary wing with no induced downwash would stall when:
base.c: Its angle relative to the horizontal total airstream reaches the critical angle
w: Effective angle of attack reaches the critical angle

base.q: After a flight, a pilot wonders: why does a low aspect ratio wing need a larger geometric angle to stall?
base.c: Downwash tilts the air so the wing feels a smaller angle than the one it is set at
w: Downwash tilts the air so the wing feels a larger angle than the one it is set at
The angle at which the wing really meets the air after downwash is taken into account
It has more tip area only

base.q: Critical effective angle 15°, downwash 6°. The geometric stalling angle is about:
A wing set at 10° with 4° of downwash feels an effective angle of:
Some very low aspect ratio delta wings have no measurable stalling angle up to:
base.c: About 40° or more

base.q: At such angles the drag is so high that the flight path is usually:
base.c: Inclined steeply downward

base.q: The super stall (deep stall) is:
base.c: A steep sinking with a shallow attitude, even though the wing may still make appreciable lift
w: A normal stall with the nose dropping
A stall of the tailplane only

base.q: Attitude means:
base.c: How the aircraft's body is tilted compared with the horizon
w: The angle between wing and oncoming air

base.q: The flight path is:
base.c: The direction in which the aircraft actually travels

base.q: Angle of attack is the angle between:
base.c: The wing (chord line) and the oncoming air (flight path)
w: The average chord along the wing
The flight path and the horizon

base.q: On a check ride the instructor asks: why is the super stall deceptive?
base.c: The body may look nearly level while the aircraft sinks and the angle of attack is large
w: The pilot cannot see the horizon

base.q: Apart from a rapid descent, a super stall may bring:
base.c: A possible loss of stability and control

base.q: In a design meeting someone asks: which is a disadvantage of high aspect ratio wings?
base.c: They increase weight and have relatively poor stiffness
w: They decrease weight and have relatively poor stiffness

base.q: Vertical gust effects on the airframe are:
base.c: Aggravated by a higher aspect ratio
w: Aggravated by a lower aspect ratio
Reduced by a higher aspect ratio

base.q: A gust is:
base.c: A sudden burst of wind

base.q: The lower the cruising speed, the:
base.c: Higher the aspect ratio that can usefully be used
w: Lower the aspect ratio that can usefully be used

base.q: Aircraft for very high-speed, especially supersonic, flight usually use:
base.c: Low-aspect-ratio planforms

base.q: Supersonic aircraft operate at:
base.c: Relatively low lift coefficients and demand great aerodynamic cleanness
w: Relatively high lift coefficients and demand great aerodynamic cleanness

base.q: An engineer sketching a new wing asks: why is a long thin wing heavier?
base.c: It bends more, like a long diving board, and needs a stronger structure
w: It bends less, like a long diving board, and needs a weaker structure

base.q: The book's memory line is:
base.c: High A = slow and efficient; low A = fast and clean
w: High A = fast; low A = slow
High A = heavy; low A = light

base.q: Taper describes:
base.c: How quickly the chord gets smaller towards the tip
w: How quickly the chord gets larger towards the root
How far it is swept back

base.q: Taper ratio λ is:
base.c: Tip chord ÷ root chord

base.q: A rectangular wing has λ =
A wing ending in a point has λ =
Root chord 8 ft, tip chord 2 ft. λ =
Root chord 6 ft, λ = 0.5. The tip chord is:
base.c: 3 ft

base.q: An engineer sketching a new wing asks: which statement is correct?
base.c: Two wings can share an aspect ratio but have different taper ratios
w: Aggravated by a higher aspect ratio
Aspect ratio and taper ratio are the same thing

base.q: The root is:
base.c: The part of the wing attached to the fuselage
w: The outer end of the wing

base.q: Local effects along the span come from:
base.c: The distribution of area along the span (taper)

base.q: C<sub>l</sub> (small l) is the lift coefficient of:
base.c: One section (slice) of the wing

base.q: C<sub>L</sub> (capital L) is the lift coefficient of:
base.c: The whole wing

base.q: A section with C<sub>l</sub>/C<sub>L</sub> = 1.5 is working:
base.c: Harder than the wing average

base.q: The natural distribution of lift along a span is roughly:
base.c: Elliptical

base.q: On the elliptical wing, C<sub>l</sub>/C<sub>L</sub> is:
base.c: 1.0 along the whole span

base.q: On the elliptical wing, the induced downflow is:
base.c: Uniform along the span

base.q: A designer comparing wing options asks: why does the elliptical wing have the least induced drag for a given aspect ratio?
base.c: Uniform lift coefficient and uniform downwash
w: The local lift coefficient is highest

base.q: The merit of any planform is measured by:
base.c: How closely its lift and downwash distribution approach the elliptical
w: Uniform lift coefficient and uniform downwash

base.q: The wing's angle of attack is made up of:
base.c: α<sub>0</sub> + α<sub>i</sub>

base.q: α<sub>0</sub> is:
base.c: The local section angle the wing really works at (it gives lift)
w: The lift and drag obtainable from a given wing area, and the stalling angle of attack

base.q: α<sub>i</sub> is:
base.c: The local induced angle (the angle taken by downwash)
w: The angle at which the wing really meets the air after downwash is taken into account

base.q: If downwash is large at some point on the span:
base.c: α<sub>i</sub> is large there, α<sub>0</sub> is smaller, and that section makes less lift
w: α<sub>i</sub> is large there, α<sub>0</sub> is larger, and that section makes more lift
More lift gives more induced drag, less lift gives less

base.q: On a rectangular wing the downwash is:
base.c: High at the tip and low at the root
w: High at the root and low at the tip

base.q: On a rectangular wing the local lift coefficient is:
base.c: Low at the tip and high at the root
w: High at the tip and low at the root

base.q: At the root of a rectangular wing the local C<sub>l</sub> is almost:
base.c: 20% greater than C<sub>L</sub>

base.q: A rectangular wing of A = 6 compared with an elliptical wing has:
base.c: 16% more induced angle and 5% more induced drag
w: 16% less induced angle and 5% less induced drag
More lift gives more induced drag, less lift gives less

base.q: The pointed wing (λ = 0):
base.c: Cannot hold the main tip vortex; downwash is greatest at the root and decreases toward the tip
w: Cannot hold the main root vortex; downwash is greatest at the tip and increases toward the root

base.q: Right next to a pointed tip there is:
base.c: Upwash (negative induced angles)

base.q: On a pointed wing the local lift coefficient is:
base.c: Low at the root and very high at the tip
w: High at the root and low at the tip

base.q: A pointed wing of A = 6 compared with elliptical has:
base.c: 17% more induced angle and 13% more induced drag
w: 17% less induced angle and 13% less induced drag
More lift gives more induced drag, less lift gives less

base.q: A λ = 0.5 wing of A = 6 compared with elliptical has:
base.c: 3% more induced angle and 1% more induced drag
w: 3% less induced angle and 1% less induced drag
More lift gives more induced drag, less lift gives less

base.q: The usual taper ratio range is:
A designer comparing wing options asks: why are real wings tapered?
base.c: For structural weight and stiffness
w: They increase weight and have relatively poor stiffness

base.q: An engineer sketching a new wing asks: how is aerodynamic efficiency preserved on tapered wings?
base.c: Wing twist and section variation

base.q: The major objection to the elliptical wing is:
base.c: Extreme difficulty of mechanical layout and construction

base.q: The elliptical wing is the ideal planform for:
base.c: Subsonic flight

base.q: The desirable stall pattern is one that begins:
base.c: At the root sections first

base.q: On a check ride the instructor asks: which is an advantage of root-first stalling?
base.c: The ailerons remain effective at high angles of attack
w: The ailerons remain effective at low angles of attack
Effective angle of attack reaches the critical angle

base.q: Warning of a root stall comes from:
base.c: Buffet on the tailplane and aft fuselage

base.q: The loss of downwash behind the root usually gives:
base.c: A stable nose-down moment

base.q: A wing begins to stall where:
base.c: The local lift coefficient is highest
w: The local lift coefficient is lowest

base.q: On the elliptical wing, the stall:
base.c: Begins and progresses uniformly, with little warning

base.q: On the elliptical wing near the stall:
base.c: Ailerons may lack effectiveness and lateral control may be difficult

base.q: The rectangular wing has:
base.c: A strong root-stall tendency

base.q: The rectangular wing finds limited application mainly on:
base.c: Low-cost, low-speed light planes
w: The low-speed effects of wing planforms

base.q: A λ = 0.5 wing has a stall pattern:
base.c: Much the same as the elliptical wing

base.q: A highly tapered wing (λ = 0.25) has:
base.c: A strong tip-stall tendency

base.q: On a λ = 0.25 wing the stall starts:
base.c: At the station just inboard of the tip
w: At the station just outboard of the root

base.q: The pointed-tip wing (λ = 0):
base.c: Is effectively stalled at the tip at any lift condition unless heavily tailored
w: Is effectively stalled at the root at any lift condition unless heavily tailored

base.q: Applying sweepback alters the lift distribution like:
base.c: Decreasing the taper ratio

base.q: Inboard means:
base.c: Closer to the fuselage

base.q: Ailerons are:
base.c: Movable surfaces near the wing tips that make the aircraft roll
w: Movable surfaces near the wing roots that make the aircraft roll
The tips make up a larger share of the wing

base.q: Buffet is:
base.c: Shaking caused by turbulent, broken-up airflow
w: Shaking caused by turbulent, broken-down airflow

base.q: The elliptical wing is best for drag but:
base.c: Not best for stall behaviour

base.q: Sweepback means the wing is:
base.c: Angled backwards, like an arrow

base.q: The reason for using sweepback is:
base.c: Low drag at higher speeds
w: Higher landing speeds for a given wing loading

base.q: The cost of sweepback is:
base.c: Poorer performance at low speeds (take-off and landing)
w: Poorer performance at high speeds (take-off and landing)
Higher landing speeds for a given wing loading

base.q: The leading edge is:
base.c: The front edge of the wing

base.q: This book uses which symbol for the sweep angle?
base.c: Λ

base.q: Compared with a similar straight wing, a swept wing has:
base.c: A reduced C<sub>L max</sub> (about 30% at 45° sweep)
w: A increased C<sub>L max</sub> (about 30% at 45° sweep)
Reduced C<sub>L max</sub> and increased stalling angle

base.q: The reduction in C<sub>L max</sub> is due to:
base.c: Premature flow separation from the upper surface at the wing tips
w: Premature flow separation from the upper surface at the wing roots
Leading-edge separation, flow around the wing tips, and spanwise boundary-layer flow

base.q: Washout is:
base.c: A built-in twist making the tip meet the air at a smaller angle than the root
w: A built-in twist making the root meet the air at a larger angle than the tip
An effective angle of attack that increases from root to tip

base.q: Figure 2.4 shows that more sweep gives:
base.c: A lower lift-curve slope and lower C<sub>L max</sub>, with the peak at a larger angle of attack
w: A higher lift-curve slope and higher C<sub>L max</sub>, with the peak at a smaller angle of attack
Unstable, varying with angle of attack, causing buffet and drag, lowering C<sub>L max</sub>
A peak at a smaller angle

base.q: After a flight, a pilot wonders: which airspeed component has no effect on lift?
base.c: V1, parallel to the leading edge
w: V2, normal to the leading edge

base.q: V2 equals:
base.c: V cos Λ

base.q: The C<sub>L</sub> of a swept wing is reduced in the ratio of:
base.c: The cosine of the sweep angle
w: The sine of the sweep angle
The tangent of the sweep angle

base.q: A change Δα in fuselage incidence gives an angle-of-attack change at a swept wing of:
base.c: Δα cos Λ

base.q: At Λ = 60°, cos 60° = 0.5. The fraction of airspeed that counts toward lift is:
base.c: One half

base.q: Landing close to the lowest speed needs the wing at the angle of attack for:
base.c: C<sub>L max</sub>

base.q: After a flight, a pilot wonders: why can't a very-low-aspect-ratio swept wing use its C<sub>L max</sub> angle for landing?
base.c: Undesirable stall characteristics and an exaggerated nose-up attitude needing a long, heavy undercarriage
w: Undesirable stall characteristics and an exaggerated nose-down attitude needing a long, heavy undercarriage
A low aspect ratio, a high stalling angle and a marked nose-up attitude at the stall

base.q: The maximum touch-down angle without such measures is about:
Undercarriage means:
base.c: The landing gear (wheels and legs)

base.q: The C<sub>L</sub> at the touch-down angle compared with C<sub>L max</sub> is:
base.c: Lower

base.q: The result for swept and delta wings is:
base.c: Higher landing speeds for a given wing loading
w: Lower landing speeds for a given wing loading

base.q: Wing loading is:
base.c: Aircraft weight ÷ wing area

base.q: Weight 3000 and area 300, then the area is doubled. The wing loadings are:
base.c: 10 then 5

base.q: For a common landing speed at a stated weight, the area needed is greatest for:
base.c: The tailless delta

base.q: Figure 2.7 shows planforms with areas adjusted to give:
base.c: The same stalling speed

base.q: The book says more sweep goes with:
base.c: A reduced aspect ratio

base.q: Induced drag increases with sweep approximately in proportion to:
base.c: 1 ÷ cos Λ

base.q: At 60° sweep, 1 ÷ cos Λ is:
A pilot reviewing a stall incident asks: which is the correct chain for the extra induced drag?
base.c: Sweep lowers C<sub>L</sub>, a bigger angle of attack is needed, more downwash, more induced drag
w: Sweep lowers C<sub>L</sub>, a smaller angle of attack is needed, less downwash, less induced drag
3% more induced angle and 1% more induced drag
Sweep raises C<sub>L</sub>, smaller angle, less downwash

base.q: Compared with a straight wing, the swept wing's minimum drag speed is:
base.c: Higher

base.q: On a swept wing the approach speed is usually:
base.c: Less than the minimum drag speed
w: Greater than the minimum drag speed

base.q: The "wrong side" of the drag curve means speeds:
base.c: Below the minimum drag speed

base.q: On the wrong side, slowing down makes drag:
base.c: Rise

base.q: On the wrong side, if the pilot raises the nose slightly:
base.c: Lift rises slightly, drag rises a lot, speed falls rapidly, and a large power increase is needed
w: Lift falls slightly, drag falls a lot, speed rises rapidly, and a large power decrease is needed
Lift rises a lot and drag falls

base.q: The book warns that a stage may be reached where:
base.c: Even full power is insufficient to prevent a rapid descent

base.q: In Figure 2.8 the straight wing's lowest drag point is about at:
base.c: The approach speed

base.q: The cure used on some aircraft is to:
base.c: Increase profile drag with airbrakes or drag-chutes
w: Decrease profile drag with airbrakes or drag-chutes
A very marked increase in drag

base.q: This cure gives:
base.c: A flatter drag curve with the minimum drag speed closer to the approach speed
w: The speed at which drag starts to rise sharply because of shock waves

base.q: A further advantage of the cure is:
base.c: More power is needed on approach, giving better engine response on turbojets
w: Less power is needed on approach, giving better engine response on turbojets

base.q: Profile drag is:
base.c: Drag from the shape and surface of the aircraft

base.q: A pilot reviewing a stall incident asks: which drag does sweepback increase at high angles of attack?
base.c: Induced drag

base.q: The boundary layer is:
base.c: The thin layer of air next to the surface that is slowed by friction
w: A thick layer far from the wing

base.q: On a swept-back wing the boundary layer tends to drift:
base.c: Outward toward the wing tips
w: The tips make up a larger share of the wing

base.q: An adverse pressure gradient is:
base.c: Pressure rising in the direction of flow, which slows the air
w: Pressure falling in the direction of flow

base.q: Isobars are:
base.c: Lines joining points of equal pressure

base.q: On a check ride the instructor asks: which component of the flow is slowed by the rising pressure?
base.c: The component at right angles to the isobars
w: The component parallel to the isobars

base.q: The component parallel to the isobars is:
base.c: Unaffected, because pressure does not change along an isobar

base.q: The result at the tips is:
base.c: A pool of slow-moving air

base.q: In the ball-on-a-slope picture:
base.c: Only the uphill part of the motion is slowed

base.q: On a check ride the instructor asks: why does the drift lead to tip stalling?
base.c: It thickens the boundary layer over the outer wing, making separation easier and C<sub>L max</sub> drop suddenly at the tips
w: Leading-edge separation, flow around the wing tips, and spanwise boundary-layer flow

base.q: Leading-edge separation happens:
base.c: At high angles of attack
w: Leading-edge separation at low angles of attack

base.q: Over the inboard section the separated flow:
base.c: Re-attaches behind a short separation bubble
w: Re-attaches only at the trailing edge

base.q: Over the outboard section the separated flow:
base.c: Re-attaches only at the trailing edge or fails to attach
w: Moving the trailing edge of the wing

base.q: A separation bubble is:
base.c: A small pocket of detached flow
w: A large region of stalled flow

base.q: The ram's horn vortex is formed by:
base.c: Leading-edge separation, flow around the wing tips, and spanwise boundary-layer flow
w: Leading-edge separation, flow around the wing roots, and spanwise boundary-layer flow
Premature flow separation from the upper surface at the wing tips

base.q: The ram's horn vortex has its origin:
base.c: On the leading edge, possibly as far inboard as the wing root
w: On the leading edge, possibly as far outboard as the wing tip
The whole leading edge from root to tip

base.q: The vortex draws the air above it:
base.c: Down and behind the wing, deflecting it toward the fuselage
w: Up and behind the wing, deflecting it toward the fuselage
The part of the wing attached to the fuselage

base.q: As the angle of attack increases, the outboard ailerons:
base.c: Suffer a marked decrease in response
w: Suffer a marked increase in response

base.q: A consequence for the pilot is:
base.c: Comparatively large aileron movements are needed at low speeds and the response may be sluggish
w: Comparatively large aileron movements are needed at high speeds and the response may be sluggish

base.q: A pilot reviewing a stall incident asks: which is a cure the book names?
base.c: Move the ailerons inboard
w: At the station just inboard of the tip

base.q: An all-moving wing tip is:
base.c: A whole tip section that moves instead of a small hinged flap
w: A whole root section that moves instead of a small hinged flap
The whole leading edge from root to tip

base.q: Compared with the stall patterns section, sweepback:
base.c: Encourages the tip to stall first, the opposite of the favoured root-first pattern
w: Encourages the root to stall last, the opposite of the favoured tip-last pattern
An effective angle of attack that increases from root to tip

base.q: The crescent wing combines:
base.c: Variable sweep with a changing t/c ratio

base.q: The t/c ratio is:
base.c: Section thickness ÷ chord

base.q: At the root of a crescent wing:
base.c: The wing is thickest and the sweep is greatest

base.q: The outboard sections of a crescent wing are:
base.c: Practically unswept

base.q: Therefore at the tips there is:
base.c: Little or no outflow of the boundary layer

base.q: One advantage of the crescent wing is:
base.c: The critical drag-rise Mach number is raised
w: The critical drag-fall Mach number is lowered
The peak drag rise is reduced

base.q: Another advantage is:
base.c: The peak drag rise is reduced
w: The peak drag fall is increased
The critical drag-rise Mach number is raised
The peak drag rise is increased

base.q: A third advantage is:
base.c: Tip stalling is prevented

base.q: Mach number is:
base.c: Speed ÷ speed of sound

base.q: The critical drag-rise Mach number is:
base.c: The speed at which drag starts to rise sharply because of shock waves
w: The speed at which drag starts to fall sharply because of shock waves
The critical drag-rise Mach number is raised

base.q: A forward-swept wing has:
base.c: Tips ahead of the root

base.q: The forward-swept wing only recently became a serious alternative because of:
base.c: The behaviour of wing structures under load

base.q: The 70% chord line is taken as:
base.c: The average position for a shock wave to form near the critical Mach number
w: The critical drag-rise Mach number is raised

base.q: For the same chord-line sweep, a forward-swept wing needs:
base.c: Less leading-edge sweep
w: V1, parallel to the leading edge

base.q: The advantage of forward sweep lies in:
base.c: Better lift/drag ratio in the subsonic and near-transonic range
w: More lift gives more induced drag, less lift gives less

base.q: The disadvantage of forward sweep is:
base.c: Higher supersonic drag, bad for supersonic interception
w: Lower supersonic drag, bad for supersonic interception
Inversely proportional: higher A gives less induced drag

base.q: On a forward-swept wing the ram's horn vortex develops:
base.c: Inwards toward the root

base.q: The wing-tip vortices on a forward-swept wing:
base.c: No longer reinforce the ram's horn vortex

base.q: The ram's horn vortex on a forward-swept wing lies:
base.c: Along the fuselage (or slightly more outboard if the root is swept back)
w: Along the fuselage (or slightly less inboard if the tip is swept back)

base.q: A forward-swept wing tends to stall:
base.c: At the root first

base.q: The popular way to control forward-swept root stall is:
base.c: A canard foreplane

base.q: A canard's downwash can:
base.c: Delay root stall

base.q: The canard's vortices are used to:
base.c: Energise the airflow over the inboard wing, maintaining lift to higher angles
w: Energise the airflow over the outboard wing, maintaining lift to lower angles
Higher landing speeds for a given wing loading

base.q: The advantage of root stall is:
base.c: Aileron control is retained

base.q: The penalty of root stall is:
base.c: Directional (yaw) control may suffer because the fin and rudder sit in the turbulence

base.q: Flexure means:
base.c: Bending

base.q: On a swept-back wing, bending tends to:
base.c: Reduce the angle of attack toward the tip
w: Reduce the angle of attack toward the root
A lower stalling angle of attack

base.q: On a forward-swept wing, bending causes:
base.c: An effective angle of attack that increases from root to tip
w: An effective angle of attack that decreases from tip to root
Low at the tip and high at the root
A decrease from root to tip

base.q: Under g loading on a forward-swept wing, tip lift increases leading to:
base.c: Pitch-up as the centre of pressure moves forward
w: Pitch-down as the centre of pressure moves backward
Stability in pitch (nose up and nose down)

base.q: Aeroelastic divergence is:
base.c: A runaway loop in which airflow bends the wing and the bending increases the airflow's effect
w: A runaway loop in which airflow bends the wing and the bending decreases the airflow's effect

base.q: The result of aeroelastic divergence is likely:
base.c: Structural failure of the wing
w: The front edge of the wing

base.q: A designer comparing wing options asks: what made forward sweep practical?
base.c: Carbon-fibre technology giving controlled wing twist under load
w: The behaviour of wing structures under load

base.q: On a tailless delta the angle of attack is controlled by:
base.c: Moving the trailing edge of the wing

base.q: Raising the trailing edge:
base.c: Produces a downward force on it, increasing the angle of attack
w: Produces a upward force on it, increasing the angle of attack
A lower stalling angle of attack

base.q: Compared with the same wing with a tailplane, the tailless delta has:
base.c: Reduced C<sub>L max</sub> and increased stalling angle
w: A lower stalling angle of attack

base.q: The raised trailing edge lowers C<sub>L max</sub> because it:
base.c: Deflects air upward (less downwash) and reduces the low and high pressure areas
w: Deflects air downward (more downwash) and reduces the high and low pressure areas
Low at the root and very high at the tip

base.q: A delta planform has inherently:
base.c: A low aspect ratio, a high stalling angle and a marked nose-up attitude at the stall
w: A high aspect ratio, a low stalling angle and a marked nose-down attitude at the stall
Undesirable stall characteristics and an exaggerated nose-up attitude needing a long, heavy undercarriage

base.q: The tailless delta's apparent higher stalling angle is partly due to:
base.c: Measuring against the fixed neutral chord line by convention
w: The wing (chord line) and the oncoming air (flight path)

base.q: The stall itself, per the book, happens at:
base.c: The same angle between the actual chord line and the airflow
w: The wing (chord line) and the oncoming air (flight path)

base.q: Changes in camber affect the stalling angle:
base.c: Not appreciably

base.q: The delta wing's C<sub>L</sub> curve peak is:
base.c: Very flat

base.q: A delta's stall is:
base.c: Mild and gradual, with a gradual loss of lift

base.q: A delta can be flown above the C<sub>L max</sub> angle with:
base.c: A very marked increase in drag
w: A very marked decrease in drag
Increase profile drag with airbrakes or drag-chutes

base.c: The pilot is aware of attitude relative to the horizontal but not always of angle of attack
w: Its angle relative to the horizontal total airstream reaches the critical angle

base.q: A slender delta is:
base.c: A very narrow, pointed delta with low supersonic drag
w: A very narrow, pointed delta with high supersonic drag
A very marked increase in drag

base.q: A sharp leading edge on a slender delta produces:
base.c: Leading-edge separation at low angles of attack
w: Leading-edge separation at high angles of attack

base.q: This separation on a slender delta is, paradoxically:
base.c: Encouraged

base.q: The old view of such a vortex was that it is:
base.c: Unstable, varying with angle of attack, causing buffet and drag, lowering C<sub>L max</sub>
w: The lift and drag obtainable from a given wing area, and the stalling angle of attack

base.q: On a slender delta the vortex covers:
base.c: The whole leading edge from root to tip

base.q: The first benefit of the vortex is:
base.c: The centre of pressure is nearer mid-chord, giving better longitudinal stability
w: Pitch-up as the centre of pressure moves forward

base.q: Longitudinal stability means:
base.c: Stability in pitch (nose up and nose down)

base.q: The second benefit is:
base.c: Low pressure in the vortex core gives a C<sub>L</sub> increase of up to about 30%
w: High pressure in the vortex core gives a C<sub>L</sub> decrease of down to about 30%

w: The vortex seldom gets near the tip and its energy ends down in the wake, giving low induced drag

base.q: The wake is:
base.c: The disturbed air left behind the wing
w: The air ahead of the wing

w: Swept back at low speed and swept backward again (to nearly straight) at high speed

base.q: Supersonic aircraft usually have wings with:

base.q: Such wings at low speeds are:

base.q: A swing-wing's "swept forward again" is:

The same as a forward-swept wing

base.q: Which statement about the effective angle of attack is FALSE?

base.q: Which statement about the wrong side of the drag curve is FALSE?

A large power increase may be needed to recover

w: Induced drag is linked to producing lift
Sweepback increases induced drag at high angles of attack
Airbrakes add profile drag on purpose

Its tips stall late and hold the lift
It produces less drag than other wings

It makes less lift at every angle

The root chord is smaller than the tip chord
The tip is swept and the root is not

The tip is the thickest part of the wing

w: Sweep adds weight that cancels some lift

base.q: Why does sweep increase induced drag at a given lift?

w: It adds skin friction on the surface
It adds weight to the wing

base.q: Why is a swept wing's approach on the wrong side of the drag curve?

Its drag is zero at the approach speed
Its stalling speed is zero at the approach

It cuts induced drag to zero
It removes the sweep at low speed

w: Tip vortices pull the air outward
Gravity pulls the air toward the tips
The tips are hotter than the root

w: It adds lift to the tips
It removes the ram's horn vortex

base.q: Why do the outboard ailerons of a swept wing lose response at high angles of attack?
base.c: Spanwise flow and the vortex disturb the air over the outer wing where they sit
w: They become heavier at high angles

base.q: Why does a forward-swept wing tend to stall at the root first?
base.c: Its boundary layer drifts inward toward the root
w: Its tips are heavier than the root
It has no tip vortices at all
It has more sweep than a swept-back wing

base.q: Why can a forward-swept wing suffer aeroelastic divergence?

w: Bending lowers the tip angle of attack and unloads it
It has no stiffness at all
Its engine thrust is too strong

base.q: Why does the crescent wing avoid the tip-stall problem?

w: Its tip is the most highly swept part
Its root is the thinnest part

base.q: Why does a tailless delta have a lower C<sub>L max</sub>?

w: Its aspect ratio is very high

base.q: Why can a slender delta exploit its leading-edge vortex?

w: It is unstable and changes greatly with angle of attack
It starts at the tip only

All sections stall together with no tip effects
No stall occurs at any angle

w: Tip vortices vanish and drag drops

Wing loading is too high and area too small
